title: Cañon City Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Cañon City wells have a 51-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock makes yield and drilling cost vary by lot.
h1: Cañon City Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land around Cañon City means looking past the nearest well and into the local permit record. Within five miles, Colorado DWR records show 1,223 permitted wells. Of those, 826 are recorded as constructed, 869 report total depth, 184 report pump yield, and only 28 report static water level.

The headline numbers are favorable but not uniform: the median well is 51 feet deep and the median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute. Most permits identify an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, so conditions can change quickly between nearby properties. Records from Lincoln Park, Brookside, Park Center, and Williamsburg provide useful context, but they do not replace a site-specific well and septic evaluation.

sections.heading: Cañon City well depth depends on the mountain bedrock
sections.html:
Cañon City’s recorded wells are generally shallow by Colorado standards. The median total depth is 51 feet, with the middle half between 33 and 98 feet. Seventy-five percent are under 100 feet, while 13% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 8% between 300 and 600 feet, and 4% are deeper than 600 feet.

That spread matters when you request a drilling bid. A nearby shallow well is a useful reference, not a guarantee. The local permits are dominated by unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 1,197 wells in that category. Granite and gneiss can produce water along fractures, so two lots close together may require very different drilling depths. The deepest record is 2,200 feet, showing how far local conditions can depart from the median.

sections.heading: What Cañon City wells produce for a household
sections.html:
Among the 184 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half runs from 5.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-eight percent report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 28% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Twenty-two percent fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 2% are under 1 gallon per minute.

A well producing 10.0 gallons per minute is usually a solid starting point for normal household use, but the yield test and storage system still matter. A low-producing well can sometimes serve a home with adequate tank storage, while a high-producing well does not remove the need for proper casing, grout, pump sizing, and water-quality testing. Colorado exempt household-use wells have a 35-gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: The Cañon City water table is not well documented
sections.html:
Only 28 permitted wells near Cañon City report a static water level, so the water-level record is limited. In those reports, the median depth to water is 58 feet, with the middle half between 16 and 108 feet. That range is wide enough to affect drilling method, pump setting, trenching, and the cost of bringing water into a house.

The available facts do not provide a water-level series by decade, so they do not establish that the local water table is dropping or rising. Treat the 58-foot median as a planning reference rather than a promise for a specific parcel. Ask for the well construction report, static level, pumping test, and recovery information for the subject property and nearby wells in Lincoln Park, Brookside, or Park Center.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long activity around Cañon City
sections.html:
Well permitting has continued in the Cañon City area through 2025. The records list 9 permits from the 1950s, 14 from the 1960s, 68 from the 1970s, 138 from the 1980s, 389 from the 1990s, 217 from the 2000s, 113 from the 2010s, and 77 from the 2020s.

The most active driller names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 445 wells; Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.), with 80; and Young'S Drilling & Pump Serv (Young, Nolen), with 65. Those counts describe permit records, not recommendations or current availability. A buyer should still confirm licensing, recent references, what the bid includes, and whether the proposed work is a new permit, a replacement, or a repair.

sections.heading: Cañon City drilling cost rises quickly with depth
sections.html:
Local cost planning should account for fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The drilling model uses a typical rate of $65-$100 per foot. At the 51-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,300-$5,100.

That is not the full water-system price. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,300-$17,100 at the median depth. A lot requiring a 300-foot or deeper hole will not fit that median-depth allowance, and difficult access or extra casing can change the bid. Get a written scope showing drilling, casing and grout, development, yield testing, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, permits, and any water treatment separately.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Cañon City
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are the main physical uncertainties in fractured bedrock. The records show that 2% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, while the depth range reaches 2,200 feet. Before closing, review neighboring construction reports and ask a driller what happens if the first target produces little or no water.

Water quality also deserves direct testing. Within about 10 miles, the mapped record includes 31 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 88 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped locations do not prove a problem on your parcel, but they justify testing for the contaminants relevant to the property’s location and history. Keep the well and septic system properly separated, confirm suitable building areas, and verify that septic soils, setbacks, access, and drainage work before committing to a house plan.

sections.heading: A practical Cañon City lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not a countywide average. Search the DWR permit map for wells on the property and nearby properties in Lincoln Park, Brookside, Park Center, Williamsburg, Rockvale, and Florence. Compare reported depth, yield, static water level, aquifer description, construction, and well use. The local records include domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, so use only comparable household wells when estimating a future home system.

For a new build, make the offer or due-diligence period long enough to confirm the well permit path, drilling access, septic design, and water-quality testing. If the basin is over-appropriated, an augmentation plan may be needed for some uses. Have a Colorado well contractor and septic professional review the site before you assume a shallow nearby well means an inexpensive or dependable water supply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Cañon City?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within five miles of Cañon City is 51 feet. The middle half range from 33 to 98 feet, and 75% are under 100 feet. Conditions vary sharply in fractured mountain bedrock: 4% are deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest record is 2,200 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Cañon City?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 51-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $3,300-$5,100. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $9,300-$17,100 at that depth. Deeper drilling, access, casing, and site conditions can increase the price.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Cañon City?
faq.a: Among 184 reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0-15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-eight percent produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Reported results range lower and higher, so a nearby well does not guarantee the same yield on your lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Cañon City?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit record alone. Within about 10 miles, records show 31 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 88 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove contamination at your property, but they support testing for PFAS, metals, and other site-relevant contaminants before use.

faq.q: Are Cañon City wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not show a water-level trend by decade. Only 28 wells report static water level; the median depth to water is 58 feet, with a middle half of 16-108 feet. That limited sample cannot establish a falling water table. Review the subject well’s recovery and pumping records and nearby comparable wells.
